{{Short description|Comparisons in quantitative sciences}}
{{More footnotes|date=March 2011}}

In any [[quantitative science]], the terms '''relative change''' and '''relative difference''' are used to compare two [[quantities]] while taking into account the "sizes" of the things being compared, i.e. dividing by a ''standard'' or ''reference'' or ''starting'' value.<ref name="International Electrotechnical Vocabulary z730">{{cite web | title=IEC 60050 — Details for IEV number 112-03-07: "relative" | website=International Electrotechnical Vocabulary | url=https://www.electropedia.org/iev/iev.nsf/display?openform&ievref=112-03-07 | language=ja | access-date=2023-09-24}}</ref> The comparison is expressed as a [[ratio]] and is a [[unitless]] [[number]]. By multiplying these ratios by 100 they can be expressed as [[percentage]]s so the terms '''percentage change''', '''percent(age) difference''', or '''relative percentage difference''' are also commonly used. The terms "change" and "difference" are used interchangeably.{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985}} 

Relative change is often used as a quantitative indicator of [[quality assurance]] and [[quality control]] for repeated measurements where the outcomes are expected to be the same. A special case of percent change (relative change expressed as a percentage) called ''[[#Percent error|percent error]]'' occurs in measuring situations where the reference value is the accepted or actual value (perhaps theoretically determined) and the value being compared to it is experimentally determined (by measurement).

The relative change formula is not well-behaved under many conditions. Various alternative formulas, called ''[[#Indicators of relative change|indicators of relative change]]'', have been proposed in the literature. Several authors have found ''log change'' and '''log points''' to be satisfactory indicators, but these have not seen widespread use.<ref>{{harvnb|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985|p=11}}: "We suggest that this indicator should be used more extensively."</ref>

== Definition ==

Given two numerical quantities, {{math|''v''{{sub|ref}}}} and {{mvar|v}} with {{math|''v''{{sub|ref}}}} some ''reference value'', their ''actual change'', ''actual difference'', or ''absolute change'' is 
<math display="block">\Delta v = v - v_\mathrm{ref}.</math>
The term ''[[absolute difference]]'' is sometimes also used even though the absolute value is not taken; the sign of [[Delta_(letter)|Δ]] typically is uniform, e.g. across an increasing data series. If the relationship of the value with respect to the reference value (that is, larger or smaller) does not matter in a particular application, the absolute value may be used in place of the actual change in the above formula to produce a value for the relative change which is always non-negative. The actual difference is not usually a good way to compare the numbers, in particular because it depends on the [[unit of measurement]]. For instance, {{val|1 |ul=m}} is the same as {{val|100 |ul=cm}}, but the absolute difference between {{val|2 | and |1 |u=m}} is 1 while the absolute difference between {{val|200 | and |100 |u=cm}} is 100, giving the impression of a larger difference.{{sfn|Vartia|1976|p=9}} But even with constant units, the relative change helps judge the importance of the respective change. For example, an increase in price of {{val|p=$|100}} of a valuable is considered big if changing from {{val|p=$|50 |to |150}} but rather small when changing from {{val|p=$|10000 |to |10100|fmt=commas}}.

We can adjust the comparison to take into account the "size" of the quantities involved, by defining, for positive values of {{math|''v''{{sub|ref}}}}:
<math display="block"> \text{relative change}(v_\mathrm{ref}, v) = \frac{\text{actual change}}{\text{reference value}} = \frac{\Delta v}{v_\mathrm{ref}} = \frac{v}{v_\mathrm{ref}} - 1.</math>

The relative change is independent of the unit of measurement employed; for example, the relative change from {{val|2 |to| 1| ul=m}} is {{val|-50|u=%}}, the same as for {{val|200 |to| 100 |u=cm}}. The relative change is not defined if the reference value ({{math|''v''{{sub|ref}}}}) is zero, and gives negative values for positive increases if {{math|''v''{{sub|ref}}}} is negative, hence it is not usually defined for negative reference values either. For example, we might want to calculate the relative change of {{val|−10| to| −6}}. The above formula gives {{math|1={{sfrac|(−6) − (−10) | −10}} = {{sfrac|4 | −10}} = −0.4}}, indicating a decrease, yet in fact the reading increased.

Measures of relative change are [[unitless]] numbers expressed as a [[fraction (mathematics)|fraction]]. Corresponding values of percent change would be obtained by multiplying these values by 100 (and appending the % sign to indicate that the value is a percentage).

== Domain ==

The domain restriction of relative change to positive numbers often poses a constraint. To avoid this problem it is common to take the absolute value, so that the relative change formula works correctly for all nonzero values of {{tmath|v_\mathrm{ref} }}:
<math display="block"> \text{Relative change}(v_\mathrm{ref}, v)  = \frac{v - v_\mathrm{ref}}{|v_\mathrm{ref}|}.</math>

This still does not solve the issue when the reference is zero. It is common to instead use an indicator of relative change, and take the absolute values of both {{tmath|v}} and {{tmath| v_\mathrm{ref} }}. Then the only problematic case is {{tmath|1= v = v_\mathrm{ref} = 0}}, which can usually be addressed by appropriately extending the indicator. For example, for [[arithmetic mean]] this formula may be used:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Miller |first1=H. Ronald |title=Optimization: Foundations and Applications |date=29 March 2011 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |location=New York |isbn=978-1-118-03118-6 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HA72DsQMDnoC&pg=PA298 |language=en}}</ref>
<math display="block">d_r(x,y)=\frac{|x-y|}{(|x|+|y|)/2},\ d_r(0,0)=0 .</math>

==Percentage change==

A '''percentage change''' is a way to express a change in a variable. It represents the relative change between the old value and the new one.

For example, if a house is worth {{val|p=$|100000|fmt=commas}} today and the year after its value goes up to {{val|p=$|110000|fmt=commas}}, the percentage change of its value can be expressed as
<math display="block"> \frac{110,000-100,000}{100,000} = 0.1 = 10\%.</math>
It can then be said that the worth of the house went up by 10%.

More generally, if {{tmath|V_1}} represents the old value and {{tmath|V_2}} the new value,
<math display="block">\text{Percentage change} = \frac{\Delta V}{V_1} = \frac{V_2 - V_1}{V_1} \times100\% .</math>

Some calculators directly support this via a {{kbd|%CH}} or {{kbd|Δ%}} function.

When the variable in question is a percentage itself, it is better to talk about its change by using [[percentage point]]s, to avoid confusion between [[relative difference]] and [[absolute difference]].

=== Percent error ===
The '''percent error''' is a special case of the percentage form of relative change calculated from the absolute change between the experimental (measured) and theoretical (accepted) values, and dividing by the theoretical (accepted) value.
<math display="block">\%\text{ Error} = \frac{|\text{Experimental}-\text{Theoretical}|}{|\text{Theoretical}|}\times 100.</math>

The terms "Experimental" and "Theoretical" used in the equation above are commonly replaced with similar terms. Other terms used for ''experimental'' could be "measured", "calculated", or "actual" and another term used for ''theoretical'' could be "accepted".  Experimental value is what has been derived by use of calculation and/or measurement and is having its accuracy tested against the theoretical value, a value that is accepted by the scientific community or a value that could be seen as a goal for a successful result.

Although it is common practice to use the absolute value version of relative change when discussing percent error, in some situations, it can be beneficial to remove the absolute values to provide more information about the result. Thus, if an experimental value is less than the theoretical value, the percent error will be negative. This negative result provides additional information about the experimental result. For example, experimentally calculating the speed of light and coming up with a negative percent error says that the experimental value is a velocity that is less than the speed of light. This is a big difference from getting a positive percent error, which means the experimental value is a velocity that is greater than the speed of light (violating the [[theory of relativity]]) and is a newsworthy result.

The percent error equation, when rewritten by removing the absolute values, becomes:
<math display="block">\%\text{ Error} = \frac{\text{Experimental}-\text{Theoretical}}{|\text{Theoretical}|}\times100.</math>

The two values in the [[numerator]] do not [[commutative|commute]]. It is vital to preserve the order as above: subtract the theoretical value from the experimental value and not vice versa.

==Examples==

=== Valuable assets ===
Suppose that car {{mvar|M}} costs {{val|p=$|50000|fmt=commas}} and car {{mvar|L}} costs {{val|p=$|40000|fmt=commas}}. We wish to compare these costs.{{sfn|Bennett|Briggs|2005|pp=137–139}} With respect to car {{mvar|L}}, the absolute difference is {{nowrap|1= $10,000 = $50,000 − $40,000}}. That is, car {{mvar|M}} costs {{val|p=$|10000|fmt=commas}} more than car {{mvar|L}}. The relative difference is,
<math display="block">\frac{\$10,000}{\$40,000} = 0.25 = 25\%,</math>
and we say that car {{mvar|M}} costs 25% {{em|more than}} car {{mvar|L}}. It is also common to express the comparison as a ratio, which in this example is,
<math display="block">\frac{\$50,000}{\$40,000} = 1.25 = 125\%,</math>
and we say that car {{mvar|M}} costs 125% {{em|of}} the cost of car {{mvar|L}}.

In this example the cost of car {{mvar|L}} was considered the reference value, but we could have made the choice the other way and considered the cost of car {{mvar|M}} as the reference value. The absolute difference is now {{nowrap|1= −$10,000 = $40,000 − $50,000}} since car {{mvar|L}} costs {{val|p=$|10000|fmt=commas}} less than car {{mvar|M}}. The relative difference,
<math display="block">\frac{-\$10,000}{\$50,000} = -0.20 = -20\%</math>
is also negative since car {{mvar|L}} costs 20% {{em|less than}} car {{mvar|M}}. The ratio form of the comparison,
<math display="block">\frac{\$40,000}{\$50,000} = 0.8 = 80\%</math>
says that car {{mvar|L}} costs 80% {{em|of}} what car {{mvar|M}} costs.

It is the use of the words "of" and "less/more than" that distinguish between ratios and relative differences.{{sfn|Bennett|Briggs|2005|p=140}}

=== Percentages of percentages ===
If a bank were to raise the interest rate on a savings account from 3% to 4%, the statement that "the interest rate was increased by 1%" would be incorrect and misleading. The absolute change in this situation is 1 percentage point ({{nowrap|4% − 3%}}), but the relative change in the interest rate is:
<math display="block">\frac{4\% - 3\%}{3\%} = 0.333\ldots = 33\frac{1}{3}\%.</math>

In general, the term "percentage point(s)" indicates an absolute change or difference of percentages, while the [[percent sign]] or the word "percentage" refers to the relative change or difference.{{sfn|Bennett|Briggs|2005|p=141}}

== Indicators of relative change==

The (classical) relative change above is but one of the possible measures/indicators of relative change. An ''indicator of relative change'' from {{tmath|x}} (initial or reference value) to {{tmath|y}} (new value)  <math>R(x,y)</math> is a binary [[real-valued function]] defined for the domain of interest which satisfies the following properties:{{sfn|Vartia|1976|p=10}}

* Appropriate sign: <math>\begin{cases}R(x,y)> 0 &\text{iff } y>x \\ R(x,y)= 0 &\text{iff } y=x \\ R(x,y)< 0 &\text{iff } y<x \end{cases}.</math>
* {{mvar|R}} is an increasing function of {{mvar|y}} when {{mvar|x}} is fixed.
* {{mvar|R}} is continuous.
* Independent of the unit of measurement: for all {{tmath| a>0 }}, {{tmath|1= R(ax,ay) = R(x,y) }}.
* Normalized: <math display="inline">\left.\frac{d}{dy} R(1,y) \right|_{y=1} = 1</math>

The normalization condition is motivated by the observation that {{tmath|R}} scaled by a constant <math>c>0</math> still satisfies the other conditions besides normalization. Furthermore, due to the independence condition, every {{tmath|R}} can be written as a single argument function {{tmath|H}} of the ratio {{tmath| \textstyle \frac{y}{x} }}.{{sfn|Vartia|1976|p=14}} The normalization condition is then that {{tmath|1= H'(1) = 1 }}. This implies all indicators behave like the classical one when {{tmath|1= \textstyle \frac{y}{x} }} is close to {{math|1}}.

Usually the indicator of relative change is presented as the actual change {{math|Δ}} scaled by some function of the values {{mvar|x}} and {{mvar|y}}, say {{math|{{itco|''f''}}(''x'', ''y'')}}:{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985}}
<math display="block"> \text{Relative change}(x, y) = \frac{\text{Actual change}\,\Delta}{f(x,y)} = \frac{y - x}{f(x,y)}.</math>

As with classical relative change, the general relative change is undefined if {{math|{{itco|''f''}}(''x'', ''y'')}} is zero. Various choices for the function {{math|{{itco|''f''}}(''x'', ''y'')}} have been proposed:{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985|p=5}}
{| class="wikitable plainrowheaders" style="text-align: center;"
|+ Indicators of relative change{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985|p=5}}
|-
! scope="col" | Name
! scope="col" | <math>f(x,y)</math><br/>where the indicator's value is <math display="inline">\tfrac{y-x}{f(x,y)}</math>
! scope="col" | <math>H(y/x)</math>
|-
! scope="row" | (Classical) Relative change
| {{mvar|x}} || <math>\frac y x - 1</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Reversed relative change
| {{mvar|y}} || <math>1-\frac x y</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Arithmetic mean change
| <math>\frac{1}{2}(x + y)</math> || <math>\frac{\frac{y}{x} - 1}{\frac{1}{2}\left(1 + \frac{y}{ x}\right)}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Geometric mean change
| <math>\sqrt{xy}</math> || <math>\frac{\frac y x - 1}{\sqrt{xy}}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Harmonic mean change
| <math>\frac 2 {\frac 1 x + \frac 1 y}</math> || <math>\frac{\left(\frac {y} {x} - 1\right)\left(1+\frac {x} {y}\right)}{2}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Moment mean change of order {{mvar|k}}
| <math>\left[\frac{1}{2}(x^{k} + y^{k})\right]^\frac{1}{k}</math> || <math>\frac{\frac y x - 1}{\left[\frac{1}{2}\left(1+\left(\frac y x\right)^k\right)\right]^\frac{1}{k}}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Maximum mean change
| <math>\max(x,y)</math> || <math>\frac{\frac y x - 1}{\max\left(1,\frac y x\right)}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Minimum mean change
| <math>\min(x,y)</math> || <math>\frac{\frac y x - 1}{\min\left(1,\frac y x\right)}</math>
|-
! scope="row" | Logarithmic (mean) change 
| <math>\begin{cases}
\frac{y-x}{\ln\frac{y}{x}}  & x \neq y \\
x & x = y
\end{cases}</math> 
| <math>\ln\frac{y}{x}</math>
|}
As can be seen in the table, all but the first two indicators have, as denominator a ''mean''. One of the properties of a mean function <math>m(x,y)</math> is:{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985|p=5}}  {{tmath|1= m(x,y) = m(y,x) }}, which is to say that all such indicators have a "symmetry" property that the classical relative change lacks: {{tmath|1= R(x,y) = -R(y,x) }}. This agrees with intuition that a relative change from {{tmath|x}} to {{tmath|y}} should have the same magnitude as a relative change in the opposite direction, {{tmath|y}} to {{tmath|x}}, just like the relation <math display="inline">\frac y x = \frac 1 {x/y}</math> suggests.   

Maximum mean change has been recommended when comparing [[floating point]] values in [[programming language]]s for [[Equality (mathematics)|equality]] with a certain tolerance.<ref>{{cite web |last= Summit |first= Steve |date= 2005 |title= Question 14.5: What's a good way to check for 'close enough' floating-point equality? |website= comp.lang.c Frequently Asked Questions |url= http://c-faq.com/fp/fpequal.html }}</ref> Another application is in the computation of [[approximation error]]s when the relative error of a measurement is required.{{cn|date=December 2022}} Minimum mean change has been recommended for use in [[econometrics]].<ref>{{cite book |last1= Rao |first1= Potluri |last2= Miller |first2= Roger LeRoy |date= 1971 |title= Applied econometrics |location= Belmont, California |publisher= Wadsworth Pub. Co. |isbn= 978-0-534-00031-8 |page= 17 |url= https://archive.org/details/appliedeconometr0000raop/page/16/mode/2up}}</ref>{{sfn|Vartia|1976|pp=17-18}} Logarithmic change has been recommended as a general-purpose replacement for relative change and is discussed more below.

Tenhunen defines a general relative difference function from {{mvar|L}} (reference value) to {{mvar|K}}:{{sfn|Tenhunen|1990|p=20}}
<math display="block">
H(K,L) = \begin{cases}
  \int_1^{K/L} t^{c-1} dt & \text{when } K>L \\
  -\int_{K/L}^1 t^{c-1} dt & \text{when } K<L
\end{cases}
</math>

which leads to
<math display="block">
H(K,L) = \begin{cases}
  \frac{1}{c} \cdot ((K/L)^c-1) & c \neq 0 \\
  \ln(K/L) & c = 0, K > 0, L > 0
\end{cases}
</math>

In particular for the special cases {{math|1= ''c'' = ±1}},
<math display="block">
H(K,L) = \begin{cases}
  (K-L)/K & c=-1 \\
  (K-L)/L & c=1
\end{cases}
</math>

==Logarithmic change==
{{see also|Logarithmic derivative}}

Of these indicators of relative change, arguably the most natural is the [[natural logarithm]] ({{tmath|\ln}}) of the ratio of the two numbers (final and initial), called ''log change''.{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985}} Indeed, when {{tmath|1= \textstyle \left{{!}} \frac{V_1 - V_0}{V_0} \right{{!}} \ll 1 }}, the following approximation holds:
<math display="block">\begin{align} \ln\frac{V_1}{V_0}
&= \int_{V_0}^{V_1}\frac{{\mathrm d}V}{V} \approx \int_{V_0}^{V_1}\frac{{\mathrm d}V}{V_0} \\
&= \frac{V_1 - V_0}{V_0},
\end{align}</math>
which is the classical relative change formula.

Because {{tmath|1= \textstyle \ln\frac{V_1}{V_0} = \ln(V_1)-\ln(V_0) }}, it follows that, when the previous condition holds, the difference between (natural) logarithms is approximately equal to the percentange change.

In the same way that relative change is scaled by 100 to get percentages, <math display="inline">\ln\frac{V_1}{V_0}</math> can be scaled by 100 to get what is commonly called '''log points'''.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Békés |first1=Gábor |last2=Kézdi |first2=Gábor |title=Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy |date=6 May 2021 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-48301-8 |page=203 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1TorEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA203 |language=en}}</ref> Log points are equivalent to the unit [[Neper|centinepers]] (cNp) when measured for root-power quantities.<ref name="Blythe2020">{{harvp|Karjus|Blythe|Kirby|Smith|2020|loc= Section A.3.1}}.</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Roe |first1=John |last2=deForest |first2=Russ |last3=Jamshidi |first3=Sara |title=Mathematics for Sustainability |date=26 April 2018 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-319-76660-7 |page=190 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3ppYDwAAQBAJ&dq=centinepers&pg=PA190 |language=en|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-76660-7_4}}</ref> This quantity has also been referred to as a log percentage and denoted {{mvar|L%}}.{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985}}
Since the derivative of the natural log at 1 is 1, log points are approximately equal to percent change for small differences{{snd}} for example an increase of 1% equals an increase of {{val|0.995|u=cNp}}, and a 5% increase gives a {{val|4.88|u=cNp}} increase. This [[approximation property]] does not hold for other choices of logarithm base, which introduce a scaling factor due to the derivative not being 1. Log points can thus be used as a replacement for percent change.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Doyle|first=Patrick|date=2016-08-24|title=The Case for a Logarithmic Performance Metric|url=https://engineering.vena.io/2016/08/24/the-case-for-a-logarithmic-performance-metric/|website=Vena Solutions}}</ref><ref name="Blythe2020"/>

=== Additivity ===

Using log change has the advantages of additivity compared to relative change.{{sfn|Törnqvist|Vartia|Vartia|1985}}<ref name="Blythe2020"/> Specifically, when using log change, the total change after a series of changes equals the sum of the changes. With percent, summing the changes is only an approximation, with larger error for larger changes.<ref name="Blythe2020"/> For example:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:right;"
|-
! scope="col" | Log change 0 (cNp)
! scope="col" | Log change 1 (cNp)
! scope="col" | Total log change (cNp)
! scope="col" | Relative change 0 (%)
! scope="col" | Relative change 1 (%)
! scope="col" | Total relative change (%)
|-
| 10 || 5 || 15 || 10 || 5 || 15.5
|-
| 10 || −5 || 5 || 10 || −5 || 4.5
|-
| 10 || 10 || 20 || 10 || 10 || 21
|-
| 10 || −10 || 0 || 10 || −10 || −1
|-
| 50 || 50 || 100 || 50 || 50 || 125
|-
| 50 || −50 || 0 || 50 || −50 || −25
|}

Note that in the above table, since "relative change 0" (respectively "relative change 1") has the same numerical value as "log change 0" (respectively "log change 1"), it does not correspond to the same variation. The conversion between relative and log changes may be computed as {{tmath|1= \text{log change} = \ln(1 + \text{relative change}) }}.

By additivity, {{tmath|1= \textstyle \ln\frac{V_1}{V_0} + \ln\frac{V_0}{V_1} = 0 }}, and therefore additivity implies a sort of symmetry property, namely <math display="inline">\ln\frac{V_1}{V_0} = - \ln\frac{V_0}{V_1}</math> and thus the [[Absolute value|magnitude]] of a change expressed in log change is the same whether {{tmath|V_0}} or {{tmath|V_1}} is chosen as the reference.<ref name="Blythe2020"/> In contrast, for relative change, {{tmath|1= \textstyle \frac{V_1 - V_0}{V_0} \neq - \frac{V_0 - V_1}{V_1} }}, with the difference <math display="inline">\frac{(V_1 - V_0)^2}{V_0 V_1}</math> becoming larger as {{tmath|V_1}} or {{tmath|V_0}} approaches {{math|0}} while the other remains fixed. For example:
{| class="wikitable" style="text-align:right;"
|-
! scope="col" | ''V''<sub>0</sub>
! scope="col" | ''V''<sub>1</sub>
! scope="col" | Log change (cNp)
! scope="col" | Relative change (%)
|-
| 10 || 9 || −10.5 || −10.0
|-
| 9 || 10 || +10.5 || +11.1
|-
| 10 || 1 || −230 || −90
|-
| 1 || 10 || +230 || +900
|-
| 10 || 0<sup>+</sup> || −∞ || −100
|-
| 0<sup>+</sup> || 10 || +∞ || +∞
|}

Here 0<sup>+</sup> means taking the [[limit from above]] towards 0.
 	
=== Uniqueness and extensions ===
The log change is the unique two-variable function that is additive, and whose linearization matches relative change. There is a family of additive difference functions <math>F_\lambda(x,y)</math> for any {{tmath|1= \lambda\in\mathbb{R} }}, such that absolute change is <math>F_0</math> and log change is {{tmath| F_1 }}.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Brauen |first1=Silvan |last2=Erpf |first2=Philipp |last3=Wasem |first3=Micha |title=On Absolute and Relative Change |journal=SSRN Electronic Journal |date=2020 |doi=10.2139/ssrn.3739890 |arxiv=2011.14807 |s2cid=227228720 }}</ref>
